summary: The Dutch brought tea to Java in the 1820s, first planting China-type bushes grown from Japanese and Chinese seed, but the industry only took hold after assamica plants from British India replaced them from the late 1870s. Most Javanese tea still comes from the volcanic Priangan highlands of West Java, south of Bandung, where estates at roughly 1,000–1,800 meters pick year-round because the equatorial climate has no real dormant season. The bulk is orthodox black tea sold at auction as a blending tea, prized for a bright, clean, coppery liquor and a light, brisk, faintly fruity character rather than depth or malt; higher-grown, carefully plucked lots can be delicate and floral. At home, most Indonesians drink tea sweetened, often as the jasmine-scented teh wangi or from bottles, and much fine leaf goes abroad.

Sumatra's tea industry grew up in the early 20th century around the large estates of North Sumatra near Pematang Siantar, alongside tobacco and rubber, and later in the Kerinci highlands of Jambi, where Kayu Aro — on the slopes of Mount Kerinci at around 1,400–1,600 meters — is often described as one of the largest single tea estates in the world. Like Java's, Sumatran tea is mostly orthodox black from assamica bushes picked year-round, destined largely for export blends. It tends to be somewhat fuller and stronger than Java tea, with more body and malty depth, which makes it a common base in breakfast-style blends.
